name: John Wesley
role: Anglican priest, evangelist, founder of Methodism
summary: Anglican priest whose itinerant preaching and network of societies launched the Methodist movement in Britain and America.

key_dates.label: Ordained priest in the Church of England
Sails as a missionary to Georgia (returns 1737–38)
Aldersgate Street experience: "I felt my heart strangely warmed" (24 May)
Begins open-air field preaching at Bristol
Ordains preachers for America and signs the Deed of Declaration

accomplishments.text: With his brother Charles led a small Oxford group, mocked as the "Holy Club" and "Methodists," devoted to prayer, study, and visiting prisoners.
Recorded in his Journal his experience at a meeting in Aldersgate Street on 24 May 1738, where he felt assured of salvation by faith in Christ.
Took up open-air preaching in 1739 at George Whitefield's urging and traveled an estimated 250,000 miles on horseback over five decades.
Organized converts into societies, classes, and bands, with lay preachers and an annual Conference beginning in 1744.
Taught Christian perfection: that believers can be made perfect in love in this life.
Published sermons, tracts, and a Christian Library for ordinary readers, and with Charles produced hymnbooks for the movement.
Ordained Thomas Coke as superintendent for American Methodists in 1784, opening the way for the Methodist Episcopal Church.
Spoke against the slave trade; his Thoughts upon Slavery (1774) and his final known letter (1791, to William Wilberforce) urged its abolition.

persecution_note: Wesley was never imprisoned or executed. He faced a lawsuit and a grand jury indictment in colonial Georgia, was shut out of many Church of England pulpits, and was attacked by mobs during the early years of Methodism.

persecution.title: Indicted in Savannah, Georgia
persecution.summary: Wesley refused Holy Communion to Sophia Williamson (née Hopkey), whom he had courted before her marriage. Her husband, William Williamson, sued him for defaming her, and a warrant was issued for Wesley. A grand jury in Savannah, encouraged by her uncle Thomas Causton, the town's chief magistrate, indicted him on ten counts, most about how he ran the church. Wesley argued that a civil court had no authority over church matters.

responsible.name: Thomas Causton
responsible.role: Chief magistrate of Savannah; Sophia's uncle; pressed the case
responsible.jurisdiction: Province of Georgia (British colony governed by the Trustees)

persecution.outcome: He was never tried. He left Georgia in December 1737 and returned to England.

persecution.title: Shut out of church pulpits; told to leave the Diocese of Bristol
persecution.summary: As his preaching became controversial, many Church of England clergy refused to let him preach in their churches, which pushed him into preaching in the open air. In August 1739 Joseph Butler, Bishop of Bristol, told Wesley that he had no business preaching in the diocese and advised him to leave.

responsible.name: Joseph Butler
responsible.role: Bishop of Bristol; told him to leave the diocese
responsible.jurisdiction: Diocese of Bristol, Church of England

persecution.outcome: Wesley replied that he had been ordained as a fellow of Lincoln College, Oxford, not to any one parish, so he could preach anywhere. He continued.

persecution.title: Seized by a mob at Wednesbury
persecution.summary: Methodists around Wednesbury, Staffordshire, had been attacked by mobs for months. On the night of 20 October 1743, a mob seized Wesley and took him before two local justices of the peace, Justice Lane of Bentley and Justice Persehouse of Walsall, both of whom refused to deal with him. A Walsall mob then dragged him through the streets and struck him. Wesley, and later historians, accused some local clergy of encouraging the mobs.

responsible.name: Mobs from Wednesbury, Darlaston, and Walsall
Justices Lane and Persehouse
responsible.role: Local magistrates; declined to act when he was brought before them

persecution.outcome: He escaped with minor injuries after some of the crowd turned to protect him.

excommunication_note: Wesley was never excommunicated. Many clergy closed their pulpits to him, but the Church of England never took formal action against him, and he died a priest of that church. The Methodists separated from the Church of England only after his death.

sources.citation: John Wesley, The Journal of the Rev. John Wesley, ed. Nehemiah Curnock, 8 vols. (London: Charles H. Kelly, 1909–1916).
Henry D. Rack, Reasonable Enthusiast: John Wesley and the Rise of Methodism (London: Epworth Press, 1989).
